sentences.text: Walk through any major airport at sunrise and you'll notice something strange.
Hundreds of airlines, from dozens of countries, each with its own logo and its own identity.
And yet, almost every one of their aircraft wears the same basic colour: white.
It isn't an accident, and it isn't just fashion.
Behind that plain coat of paint sits a whole stack of decisions about physics, money and safety.
Some of the reasons you'll hear online are completely true.
Some are only half true.
And at least one of them is probably a myth.
So let's find out why airplanes really are white, and which explanations actually hold up.
An airliner spends a huge part of its life in direct sunlight.
It sits on open aprons for hours, waits on hot taxiways, and flies above the clouds, where nothing ever shades it.

sentences.text: Sunlight carries a surprising amount of energy, as ultraviolet, visible light and infrared.
When that energy hits a surface, some of it bounces off, and the rest is absorbed and turned into heat.
A dark surface absorbs most of it.
A white surface reflects most of it straight back into the sky.
You've probably felt this yourself.
On a summer afternoon, a black car can be too hot to touch, while a white car parked right next to it is merely warm.
For an aircraft, the difference matters most on the ground.
At cruising altitude, the outside air is usually colder than minus forty degrees, so heat is rarely a problem up there.
But parked at a gate in the desert sun, a dark fuselage would soak up heat for hours.
That heat flows into the cabin, so the air conditioning has to work harder before passengers even board.
White keeps the cabin cooler, and that means less energy spent on cooling while the aircraft waits.
Heat is also hard on the aircraft itself.
For decades, airliners were built mostly from aluminium.
Today, the newest designs are different.
The Boeing 787 is about half composite material by weight, and the Airbus A350 is even more than that.
sentences.say: The Boeing seven eighty-seven is about half composite material by weight, and the Airbus A three fifty is even more than that.

sentences.text: Those composites are mostly carbon fibre, held together by a hard plastic resin.
They're strong and light, but the resin is sensitive to both heat and ultraviolet light.
Over time, too much of either can weaken it.
That's why composite surfaces can't be left bare. They have to be painted and protected.
A light topcoat does two jobs at once: it blocks the sun's ultraviolet light, and it keeps the structure cooler.
Even the most famous jet in the world ran into this problem.
In 2022, the U.S. Air Force shelved a proposed dark blue paint scheme for the next Air Force One.
A thermal study found that the darker colour could push a small number of components past their qualified temperature limits.
The debate returned in 2026, when a new red, white, gold and dark blue design was approved.
sentences.say: The debate returned in twenty twenty-six, when a new red, white, gold and dark blue design was approved.

sentences.text: Dark paint isn't impossible on an aircraft. It simply comes with heat that engineers have to account for.
But the most dramatic example of all flew at twice the speed of sound.
Concorde cruised at around Mach 2, more than two thousand kilometres an hour.
sentences.say: Concorde cruised at around Mach two, more than two thousand kilometres an hour.

sentences.text: At that speed, the air itself became a source of heat.
Compression and friction warmed the whole airframe, and the tip of the nose reached about 127 degrees Celsius.
sentences.say: Compression and friction warmed the whole airframe, and the tip of the nose reached about a hundred and twenty-seven degrees Celsius.

sentences.text: To cope, Concorde wore a special white paint, reported to be about twice as reflective as ordinary airliner white.
And then, in 1996, Air France painted one of its Concordes blue, for a Pepsi advertising campaign.
sentences.say: And then, in nineteen ninety-six, Air France painted one of its Concordes blue, for a Pepsi advertising campaign.

sentences.text: The engineers kept the wings white, and the blue aircraft was limited to about twenty minutes at Mach 2 at a time.
sentences.say: The engineers kept the wings white, and the blue aircraft was limited to about twenty minutes at Mach two at a time.

sentences.text: After the promotion, it went back to white.
So the first reason is pure physics.
White reflects the sun, protects the materials, and keeps the heat under control.
It is the strongest reason of all, and it is completely real.
Now for a claim you'll find almost everywhere.
White paint, people say, is lighter than coloured paint, so white planes burn less fuel.
It sounds neat, but the evidence behind it is thin.
Paint does weigh something.
Estimates for a full livery on a jumbo jet range from roughly two hundred and fifty to five hundred kilograms.
But that weight depends mostly on how much paint goes on, how many layers and how much of the surface they cover, not on the colour itself.
A complex, multicoloured livery usually means more layers, more masking and more hours in the hangar.
And the lightest option of all is no paint at all.
For decades, American Airlines flew its jets in polished bare aluminium, partly to save weight and fuel.
Cathay Pacific tried the same trick on a Boeing 747 freighter.
sentences.say: Cathay Pacific tried the same trick on a Boeing seven forty-seven freighter.

sentences.text: Stripping its paint saved around two hundred kilograms, which the airline estimated was worth about one hundred and ninety-five thousand dollars a year in fuel.
But bare metal has to be polished again and again, and that labour often ate up the savings.
And composite aircraft can't fly bare at all, which is one reason American Airlines switched to a painted livery in 2013.
sentences.say: And composite aircraft can't fly bare at all, which is one reason American Airlines switched to a painted livery in twenty thirteen.

sentences.text: The real money story isn't the weight of the paint.
It's how long the paint lasts.
Sunlight slowly breaks down pigments.
Bright colours fade and turn chalky, and an aircraft can start to look tired years before its paint is actually worn out.
White fades more gracefully, so a white fuselage can stay presentable for longer.
That matters, because repainting an airliner is a big job.
Airlines typically strip and repaint each aircraft every five to seven years or so.
Depending on the aircraft, the work can keep it in the hangar for one to three weeks.
For a widebody, a full repaint is commonly quoted at one hundred and fifty to three hundred thousand dollars.
And every day in the paint shop is a day the aircraft isn't flying passengers and earning money.
So the economic case for white is not lighter paint.
It's paint that stays looking good for longer, and costs less to keep that way.
Every airliner is inspected constantly.
Pilots and engineers walk around it before flights, and it goes through deeper checks in the hangar.
They're looking for dents, cracks and corrosion, and for the dark streaks left by leaking oil or hydraulic fluid.
On a clean white surface, those problems stand out.
A streak of oil on white is hard to miss.
The same streak on a dark blue panel can be much harder to see, especially at night, under a flashlight.
Dents catch the light differently, and the edges of panels and rows of rivets are easier to follow.
Industry sources describe this as a genuine practical advantage, even though it is hard to put a number on it.
It isn't the main reason planes are white.
But maintenance teams benefit from it every single day.
And on an aircraft, catching small problems early is exactly the point.
Bird strikes are a real hazard for aviation.
Thousands are reported every year in the United States alone.
Most are harmless, but a few are serious.
In 2009, geese knocked out both engines of US Airways Flight 1549, which ended up landing on the Hudson River.
sentences.say: In two thousand nine, geese knocked out both engines of US Airways flight fifteen forty-nine, which ended up landing on the Hudson River.

sentences.text: You'll often hear that planes are painted white so that birds can see them and get out of the way.
The science on this is far less certain.
Birds see colour differently from us, and many species can see ultraviolet light.
In 2011, a team led by biologist Esteban Fernández-Juricic compared bird strike records with airline colour schemes.
sentences.say: In twenty eleven, a team led by biologist Esteban Fernandez Hurisitch compared bird strike records with airline colour schemes.

sentences.text: For three of the seven aircraft types they studied, brighter fuselages were linked to fewer strikes.
Their idea was that a bright aircraft contrasts more with the sky, so birds might spot it sooner.
But the researchers called their results suggestive, not proof.
Since then, much of the research has focused on aircraft lights rather than paint.
So white might help a little with birds.
But that isn't why airlines choose it, and as a safety feature it remains unproven.
Here's a reason most passengers never think about.
Many airlines don't actually own the planes they fly.
Roughly half of the world's commercial aircraft are leased.
Airlines rent them from leasing companies, often for years at a time.
When a lease ends, the aircraft moves on to a new operator, sometimes on the other side of the world.
A new operator means a new look.
If the plane is mostly white, the job is relatively simple.
Repaint the tail, the engines and the titles, and most of the fuselage can often stay as it is.
A fully coloured fuselage may have to be stripped and repainted from nose to tail.
That costs money, and it keeps the aircraft out of service while the work is done.
So lessors, and buyers on the second hand market, tend to prefer white.
A white aircraft is easier to hand over to the next customer.
The same logic helps airlines themselves.
New airlines, mergers and rebrands all move faster on a white canvas.
In fact, a white fuselage with a bold tail has become the standard template of airline branding.
There are exceptions.
Some airlines choose deep blues, bright greens or even all-black special schemes, and accept the extra cost.
For them, the livery is a flying billboard, and the advertising is worth it.
But for most of the industry, white is the default for a simple reason.
It keeps options open.
So why are airplanes white?
Mainly because white reflects the sun, protecting the airframe and keeping the cabin cooler.
It fades gracefully, it makes damage easier to spot, and it lets an aircraft change hands with a simpler repaint.
The paint isn't really lighter, and the birds probably weren't consulted.
But the next time you see a row of white jets at sunrise, you'll know that plain colour is one of the smartest engineering choices in the sky.
